# The Moment of Revelation

> "Our soul has escaped like a bird out of the fowler's snare. The snare is broken, and we have escaped."
>
> — Psalm 124:7

Some time in the first three weeks after he stops, a man usually has what this method calls the moment of revelation.

It's hard to describe and you can't mistake it. The day looks brighter. Up to then you've been *telling* yourself that you don't need the habit. In this moment you find you no longer have to tell yourself anything. The last thread has gone. You know that you'll live the rest of your life without it and never want it back. From then on you look at men who are still in the trap and feel only pity.

Augustine, who had fought his lust for years, wrote of the moment the fight ended: "a light as it were of serenity infused into my heart". The psalmist had his own picture of it. The bird is out, and the snare lies broken on the ground behind it.

Men who stop by willpower rarely get this moment. They're glad they've stopped, but they go through life believing they gave something up, so there's never a day when the weight comes off.

The deeper in you were, the better the moment is, and it doesn't wear off. Most joys fade. You remember that your wedding day or your first pay packet was wonderful, but you can't call the feeling back. This one you can. On a grey afternoon years from now you'll be able to stop and think, "I don't do that any more," and feel glad again. A man on a recovery forum said it simply: "I feel less depressed and more free you know."

## When does it come? {-}

For most men it's days, not weeks.

For me it came on the first day, as I told you in Chapter 20. With some readers it happens before the book is finished. Somewhere in the middle chapters they put it down and say, "That's enough. I can see the whole thing. I'm done." If you've followed every instruction and understood the trap completely, there's no reason it shouldn't happen to you straight away.

Chapter 21 said that the leftover itch fades over a few weeks and that the worst of the reminders are over in a few days. Those figures are useful, but they cause two problems.

The first is that they plant an idea: "So I'm to suffer for somewhere between five days and three weeks." You aren't.

The second is that they set a date. A man thinks, "If I can just reach day twenty-one, I'll get my reward." He has a pleasant three weeks, and then on day twenty-two he gets one of those rotten days that everybody gets, which have to do with his job or his car or his mother-in-law and nothing to do with the habit. He was waiting for fireworks and he got a wet Tuesday. That can knock the confidence out of him.

Yet if I gave you no idea at all, you might spend the rest of your life waiting for something to happen. That's what most willpower quitters do.

So here is what the two figures mean. They're a rough guide and no more.

**About five days in,** the habit stops being the main thing on your mind. This is when most men have their moment. It usually comes in one of the old danger spots: the empty house, the sleepless night, the evening after a row. You get to the far side of it and suddenly realise that you coped perfectly well, or even enjoyed yourself, and that the thought of jerking off never crossed your mind. After that it's plain sailing, and you know you're free.

**About three weeks in** is when most willpower attempts die, and it's worth knowing why.

## The three-week trap {-}

By the third week the man senses that the desire has gone. He isn't sure, so he decides to prove it. "I'll just see. If it does nothing for me, I'll know I've beaten it."

And it does feel odd. It's flat and a bit silly, and he takes that as his proof. But he has just handed the Little Monster its first meal in three weeks. Within the hour a small voice starts up: "You haven't beaten it. You want another."

He doesn't go straight back, because he's no fool and doesn't want to get hooked. He lets a safe-looking gap go by. Then the next temptation comes, and this time he has an answer ready: "I did it once and didn't get hooked. So where's the harm?"

He's already on the slope.

So don't prove anything to anyone, including yourself. You will never need to test your freedom, and every test of it is the habit under another name.

## Don't wait for it {-}

The answer is not to sit waiting for the moment of revelation. The answer is to see that it's finished from the moment you decide. You've cut off the Little Monster's supply. Nothing on earth can stop you being free now, unless you sit moping or wait for a sign.

A man who waits for a feeling is saying, "I'm not free yet." He checks himself each morning, like a child pulling up a seed to see if it's grown. The moment comes to men who've stopped looking for it, halfway through an ordinary day.

If you're a Christian you have firmer ground than a feeling. Paul says that if anyone is in Christ, "he is a new creation. The old things have passed away." He wrote that as a fact about you, and the feeling will catch up with the fact. A Catholic teacher gives the purpose of it all in one line: "Chastity is the virtue that frees you to love." You're being freed for something as well as from something.

So go and enjoy your life, and cope with it, from the very start.

The moment will arrive soon enough.
